feed.title: CyberBiota3
feed.subtitle: Building, operating, and learning in a home lab.

entry.title: Thirty-two roles on one home lab

link.title: Thirty-two roles on one home lab

entry.content:
The live CyberBiota3 configuration already had 14 agent IDs when we began the upgrade. That made replacing it a migration problem: the Telegram-bound coordinator and the older workflows still had jobs to do.

I approved designing the new structure offline first. It used 32 roles, with exact IDs and explicit delegation paths. Only the existing coordinator, main, shared its name with the new structure.

Give each role a bounded job

The design grouped work into eight departments: security operations, network operations, help desk, Linux, Docker, databases, the AI platform, and backup and recovery. Together they contained 30 roles. The coordinator and an independent governance role brought the total to 32.

The split was ten core identities and 22 on-demand specialists. “Core” meant an identity the system could address. It didn’t mean a continuously running model or a new heartbeat job.

A database question illustrates the intended route:

Owner
  → main
    → dba-lead
      → dba-performance

The coordinator could delegate to a department lead. A lead could delegate to its registered specialists. Specialists couldn’t spawn their own teams. Governance had no children and could review evidence without approving a change.

That structure put a limit on how far a request could spread. The candidate required explicit agent IDs, allowed two delegation edges below the coordinator, and started with one concurrent run. A graph check looked for unreachable roles, cycles, and paths that exceeded the depth limit.

A workspace isn’t the whole boundary

Each new role had a separate workspace and state directory. The candidate also specified a Docker sandbox, read-only workspace access, no sandbox network, a read-only root filesystem, dropped capabilities, and explicit denial of shell and modifying tools.

The production registration later recorded these settings for the 31 newly added roles:

{
  "mode": "all",
  "scope": "agent",
  "workspaceAccess": "ro",
  "docker": {
    "network": "none",
    "readOnlyRoot": true,
    "capDrop": ["ALL"],
    "memory": "512m",
    "cpus": 1
  }
}

This is an excerpt of the recorded configuration, not a complete deployable file. The per-role tool rules were another part of the restriction. A later live test inspected a running sandbox to check that the network, root-filesystem, capability, CPU, and memory settings were actually applied.

Keep the migration count honest

The three database IDs were checked for collisions and explicitly ratified. The older roles were mapped in the design, but that mapping didn’t authorize deleting them.

At production cutover, 31 new roles were added beside the existing configuration. main became the shared coordinator for the new delegation paths, and the 13 other legacy roles were preserved. The live registry therefore contained 45 IDs: 32 belonging to the 3.5 structure, including main, plus 13 preserved legacy IDs.

That count doesn’t show 45 active workers, nor does it establish identical permissions across the old and new roles. The new sandbox settings were recorded per new role; the legacy configuration was deliberately preserved.

Test the rules after the configuration passes

The offline candidate passed OpenClaw’s schema validator and the project checks for role counts, delegation edges, and forbidden tools. Runtime tests then asked different questions: could a role read another workspace, access the credential store, or skip the hierarchy?

Those attempts were denied in the staging pilot. The allowed coordinator-to-lead route succeeded. The next post covers the complication behind that success: the local model didn’t complete the multi-step delegation task, and the working pilot used a cloud coordinator with local specialists.
entry.summary: The upgrade divided operations into leads and specialists, then tested who could read, delegate, and execute.

entry.title: A backup archive finally became a running database

link.title: A backup archive finally became a running database

entry.content:
Earlier in the CyberBiota3.5 work, we had extracted backup files and checked their hashes. The OpenClaw archive also passed a listing check that found PostgreSQL table objects.

The next stage went further. Could a dump from the daily backup actually restore into a running database?

Start with the database footprint

The audit had found five PostgreSQL instances, plus MariaDB and Redis or Valkey services. The new database adapters exposed fixed statistics: connections, locks, sizes, cache-related views, and persistence status. They didn’t need application rows to answer those operational questions.

At the measured checkpoint, PostgreSQL connection use was between 6% and 12%, with no waiting locks. That didn’t justify adding PgBouncer during this upgrade. We deferred it rather than adding a connection pool without a measured need.

Backup coverage needed more work. All five PostgreSQL instances had WAL archiving disabled, so the project had no demonstrated point-in-time recovery through that mechanism. The records also lacked verified standalone daily dump timers for Gitea, Planka, and Immich. A passing backup elsewhere couldn’t cover those gaps by implication.

Restore without touching production

The functional restore used the orchestration dump from the verified daily OpenClaw archive. We extracted it into private staging, checked its SHA-256 checksum, and started an ephemeral PostgreSQL 17 container.

The container had no network, a 512 MiB memory limit, one CPU, and no production mounts. No application jobs or webhooks were attached. That kept the test database from becoming an accidental second copy of an active automation service.

The dump was restored with pg_restore, followed by ANALYZE. The checks then queried database metadata rather than printing user data.

The recorded result was:

Check Restored result
Public tables 17
Indexes 40
Populated tables 12
Database size 51 MB
Extract, checksum, startup, restore, and analysis 9.48 seconds

The source backup was taken at midnight local time that day. That timestamp identifies the recoverable snapshot used in this exercise. The 9.48 seconds measures this isolated database test; it isn’t a recovery target for the entire home lab.

The temporary container and staging files were removed after the checks. Existing backup jobs, retention settings, and production volumes were preserved.

Put recovery evidence beside the ticket

This phase also added draft service-desk classification, reviewed knowledge drafts, and a closure check requiring a human identifier and evidence references. Tests rejected the registered agent IDs when they tried to stand in for the human closer.

Those were adapter tests. They showed the intended draft and closure behavior under the tested inputs, rather than proving a deployed help-desk identity system. GLPI stayed deferred because the lab already had Leantime and Planka and the new draft helpers didn’t justify another application stack.

Keep the successful restore in its proper scope

The restored database was queryable, its indexes existed, and populated tables were present. That was stronger evidence than merely listing objects inside the dump.

It still didn’t test the application against the restored database, recover the photo library, or bring the whole machine back on replacement hardware. The recovery runbook therefore retained the missing dump coverage and WAL work as separate jobs. It also called out schema compatibility before any future image rollback: reverting an application image doesn’t by itself reverse its database migrations.

This test gave the orchestration database a concrete recovery receipt. The other applications still need their own.
entry.summary: The database stage restored a real PostgreSQL dump into an isolated engine, checked tables and indexes, and kept the untested recovery gaps on the list.

entry.title: Before adding more AI, we had to fix the host

link.title: Before adding more AI, we had to fix the host

entry.content:
At the start of the CyberBiota3.5 work, OpenClaw answered its health check while the authenticated route failed with HTTP 502. Authelia was restarting. The host also wasn’t synchronizing its clock.

That was a useful place to begin. Adding a new agent structure wouldn’t repair the service sitting in front of it.

Repair the clock and check the route again

The audit found Chrony trying to reach time sources over NTS, the authenticated time-synchronization protocol, and receiving connection refusals. The approved repair added working NTS sources and stepped the clock. The recorded correction was about 3.5 seconds.

Afterward, the host reported that its clock was synchronized. Authelia became healthy. The reliability check that had received a 502 now received a 401 on the protected route—the expected result for a request without a login. That checked something the gateway’s direct health response couldn’t: the authentication layer was responding again.

Those results support the recorded repair. They don’t establish that every possible Authelia failure comes from clock drift. Here, clock synchronization, authentication health, and the proxy retest were checked together.

Put limits around the workloads already running

Most of the running containers had no CPU or memory limit. We applied measured limits and saved them in ten Compose files, then validated all ten with docker compose config -q.

cAdvisor was the clearest before-and-after example. The first remediation receipt recorded it at 3.39 GiB before recreation and about 50 MiB afterward, with a 512 MiB limit. A later checkpoint showed about 37 MiB. These are snapshots, rather than a long-term memory benchmark, but they explain why the existing footprint needed attention.

At the first checkpoint, all 70 running containers had CPU and memory limits and none were unhealthy. After the later host work, the corresponding count was 71 of 71. Temporary agent sandboxes can change the running count, so those numbers belong to their checkpoints.

We also removed the deprecated Portainer container and 26 stale rehearsal or candidate containers. Dockhand stayed healthy. No volumes were deleted. Portainer’s Compose service was placed behind a deprecated profile, preserving a route back without leaving it running.

Make room without deleting the data

The root SSD had only about 58 GiB available in the initial audit. The project required at least 20% free space on that disk—about 93.6 GiB.

The next stage reclaimed roughly 70.6 GB of unused Docker build cache and 1.7 GB of dangling images. During the power-stability and storage work, Docker and containerd storage were moved onto the larger data SSD. The post-move record verified the bind mounts and showed the root disk at 70% used, with about 137 GiB free.

The same checkpoint recorded the battery charge cap at 80%, synchronized time after reboot, healthy Authelia and cAdvisor, and no failed system or user units. It gave us a working baseline for continuing the upgrade. It didn’t prove the cause of every earlier freeze, so the project kept a seven-day observation period for stability.

Fix the backup job too

The repository backup had been exiting with status 3. The repair added narrow exclusions for protected key, runtime, and staging paths instead of loosening their permissions. The rerun completed successfully, and restic check passed across the 44 existing snapshots. Nothing was pruned.

By the end of this stage, the lab had synchronized time, a working authentication check, bounded containers, more system-disk headroom, and a passing repository backup. The new AI work could now be tested against that baseline.
entry.summary: A drifting clock, an authentication crash loop, uncapped containers, and a nearly full system disk became the first jobs in the CyberBiota3.5 upgrade.

entry.title: Why the coordinator went to the cloud

link.title: Why the coordinator went to the cloud

entry.content:
I chose Qwen3 for CyberBiota3.5 because it was already the local model I wanted to keep using. The first inspection confirmed Ollama was serving qwen3:8b on the RTX 2070. We kept it as the local baseline rather than downloading another model to match an outdated proposal.

The tests showed where that choice worked and where the coordinator needed something else.

One correct tool call didn’t prove coordination

In the first model test, Qwen3 produced the expected typed call to network_health_query, selecting a DNS-latency query and a 15-minute window. A separate malicious-ticket test asked for secret access, firewall changes, and self-approval. The recorded response refused, with no tool calls.

The staging pilot was harder. It required the coordinator to delegate work and handle the deferred tool response. Qwen3 returned an empty disposition on that multi-step task. That failure stayed in the record.

On the same task class, the approved OpenAI OAuth model succeeded. The pilot coordinator delegated to noc-lead, and the child ran on local Qwen3 in its own Docker sandbox. That result gave us a specific reason for hybrid routing: use the cloud coordinator for the tested delegation task and retain local inference for the other roles.

It wasn’t a benchmark proving every cloud task would be better. The local cold tool-call test and the later warm role turns also had different timings and workloads, so they shouldn’t be compared as if they were the same test.

Authentication and execution were separate problems

The first unauthenticated cloud requests failed rather than switching providers. After I completed the official device-code approval for the isolated profile, the subscription catalog could be refreshed.

There was still a runtime conflict. The selected Codex harness rejected the configuration while shell execution was denied. Enabling shell access would have changed the security boundary we were trying to test.

The working configuration explicitly selected OpenClaw’s built-in runtime for the cloud model. The harmless cloud prompt then completed while tools.exec.mode remained deny. The receipt recorded a sandboxed run, the expected provider and model, and no fallback.

A follow-up request for shell execution and a host-file read was blocked. Separately, the governance role had no inherited OAuth profile and the workspaces contained no copied credential databases.

Prove the route and the refusal

The staging pilot used gpt-6-astra for the coordinator. Its allowed route to local noc-lead succeeded. A direct route from main to soc-tier1 was denied because the coordinator was required to go through the security lead.

Stopping the staging gateway left the live gateway and the existing monitoring services responsive. This let us test the coordinator without making monitoring depend on the experimental controller.

Carry the tested choice into production

The installed OpenClaw release didn’t initially include the newer 6.2 model entries in its catalog. We handled the release upgrade as a separate approved change, rather than treating a model name in a proposal as proof it was usable.

After the November 25 upgrade, the live account-scoped catalog exposed the approved model. main was changed to openai/gpt-6.2-sol through the built-in OpenClaw runtime. The default stayed ollama/qwen3:8b for the other 44 registered roles.

The final smoke recorded the expected provider and model with FALLBACK_USED=False. The checked gateway process had no OpenAI API-key environment variable, and the 31 new role directories had no duplicated OAuth credentials. Live cloud-to-local delegation succeeded, and the direct-specialist bypass was denied again.

Cloud coordination is still cloud processing; local specialist execution doesn’t make the whole request local. These receipts establish the tested route and credential checks. They don’t establish that every future task, quota response, or provider failure will behave correctly. Those remain part of operating the system after cutover.
entry.summary: Qwen3 passed a typed-tool test but failed the pilot’s multi-step delegation task. A separate runtime problem also had to be solved without enabling shell execution.

entry.title: Five incident drills, with production changes disabled

link.title: Five incident drills, with production changes disabled

entry.content:
Once the individual adapters were passing, we needed to see what happened when a problem involved more than one role. For CyberBiota3.5, we used five synthetic incident drills.

The scenarios were invented test inputs. Some read-only checks reached the live lab, but we didn’t break production to make the stories more realistic, and no drill was an actual security incident.

Assemble only the team the scenario needs

A database slowdown followed the route from main to dba-lead to dba-performance, then read live connection and lock statistics. A DNS outage used the network lead, the service specialist, a DNS check, and the monitoring probe summary.

The endpoint-event drill combined security posture, a benign forensic manifest, and an offline detection sample. Its output was a draft case and a proposed response, with execution still false.

The OpenClaw-failure drill checked whether the existing monitoring evidence remained available independently of the AI controller. The storage-pressure drill read disk and backup coverage and produced a draft request. It didn’t prune backups or delete volumes.

The Python orchestrator loaded delegation edges from the candidate manifest. Tests rejected recursive delegation, cross-department jumps, a coordinator skipping directly to a specialist, and specialists trying to spawn another worker.

These were controlled orchestration tests. The separate live gateway pilot and production smoke supplied the model-delegation evidence; the five drills weren’t five autonomous live model teams repairing the host.

Repeat the request and limit the retries

Each scenario was replayed with the same run identifier. Tickets, cases, and change requests were deduplicated instead of creating another set of records.

The runner also imposed budgets. A flaky backend hit its circuit breaker after three attempts: the initial request and two retries. A test with a two-call tool budget refused the third call. Configuring three concurrent runs was rejected; the exercised limits were serial execution or at most two total runs.

That mattered on a laptop with one local GPU. A failed backend shouldn’t create an expanding queue of reasoning jobs.

A valid delegation path can’t authorize a forbidden action

The negative tests sent prohibited requests through otherwise valid coordinator-to-lead-to-specialist chains. Shell execution, live IP blocking, volume deletion, backup pruning, container management, and self-approval were refused.

The approval component had its own checks outside the language model. It compared the human approver, allowed target and operation, canonical change-packet digest, signature, expiry, and single-use nonce. Tests rejected altered parameters, a forged signature, expired approval, replay, and attempts to use an agent identity as the approver.

Even the correctly signed test packet remained in dry-run mode. The verifier did not grant a production executor permission to act.

What the passing suite meant

By this point the combined Python suite contained 37 passing tests across monitoring, security, inventory, databases, service desk, and incident orchestration.

That result was useful because it included refusals and failure handling, not just successful queries. It was still a finite test suite. It didn’t independently certify the security of every interface or establish a working production remediation service.

The production executor remained disabled. The next stage could register the roles and test the live coordinator without quietly turning these draft workflows into autonomous host administration.
entry.summary: We exercised small incident teams, duplicate handling, forbidden actions, and an approval verifier that stayed outside the model—and in dry-run mode.

entry.title: Teaching the new tools to read the lab

link.title: Teaching the new tools to read the lab

entry.content:
CyberBiota already had monitoring before the 3.5 upgrade. The discovery pass found VictoriaMetrics, vmalert, Alertmanager, Grafana, Loki, Alloy, and Blackbox Exporter running. NetBox held inventory, and AdGuard handled DNS.

The new work was to give the project small, testable ways to read those systems. We didn’t add another polling stack.

Ask a specific question

The first Python adapter set covered host and container health, bounded logs, network metrics, DNS and TLS checks, database health, backup status, restore evidence, and draft tickets.

Instead of taking an arbitrary monitoring query, network_health_query accepted a named query template. The probe helper accepted approved targets. The database helper exposed fixed health views rather than arbitrary SQL. The container view omitted environment variables.

That made the interfaces useful to test. An argument either selected a supported operation or was rejected. The tests included arbitrary URLs, SQL text, shell fragments, and free-form metric queries; those inputs were denied.

The common adapter code also applied output limits and redaction. It capped responses at 64 KiB, recorded calls in a restricted audit log, and returned unavailable when a backend couldn’t be reached. An unavailable result had to remain visible to the caller.

Follow one failed probe through to a draft

The first monitoring drill used a deliberately closed local port. Blackbox Exporter reported probe_success=0. The adapter created a draft ticket and recorded that no external notification had been sent.

Replaying the same idempotency key returned a deduplicated result. A check against the working target then returned probe_success=1.

That sequence tested failure detection, draft creation, repeat handling, and the contrasting healthy probe. It didn’t simulate a real customer outage or prove that an agent repaired a service. Nothing was automatically restarted.

The live integration checks also looked for fresh telemetry, read an Alertmanager summary, retrieved a small bounded log sample, and checked selected host, container, database, and backup metadata. The first combined set passed 11 tests.

Compare inventory with what the host reports

The next stage added NetBox inventory queries and a redacted configuration diff. The inventory reconciliation compared the host’s passively observed addresses with a sample from NetBox. Both observed host addresses were represented in that sample.

That result was about this host and that inventory sample. It didn’t show that every device on the home network was accurately inventoried.

The diff adapter read only approved configuration files. Tests rejected traversal into other paths, secret-file requests, invalid revisions, and unauthorized role IDs. The purpose was to explain a configuration change without returning a raw checkout full of unrelated settings.

There was also a documentation mismatch worth resolving before writing this post: one phase report described a broader set of authorized NOC names than the implementation’s role allowlist. The shared adapter code has the narrower list. I haven’t treated the longer report table as proof that those extra roles have access.

Leave network visibility gaps visible

The Dell was connected over Wi-Fi. There was no authorized switch-mirror feed, no live packet sensor, and no approved set of switch polling targets in this work.

We deferred Zabbix, Oxidized, SmokePing, and continuous flow tooling because the existing stack covered the approved questions or the hardware and network setup didn’t justify the addition.

The Python tests reached live backends. The later gateway tests proved selected role routing and sandbox behavior. Those are separate results: this work doesn’t yet demonstrate a real Telegram incident using every adapter end to end. The next step is to collect that evidence during actual use, without changing the meaning of the tests we already have.
entry.summary: The monitoring work reused VictoriaMetrics, Loki, NetBox, and existing probes, then added bounded Python adapters for specific operational questions.

entry.title: Putting CyberBiota3.5 into production
entry.content:
By late November 24, the offline design, staging pilot, adapter tests, and restore exercises had their validation records. The operating handoff had also been written. It still described the production cutover as future work.

The project then continued through separately approved changes. That sequence matters when reading the files: the later cutover receipts supersede the handoff’s statement about production still being untouched.

Add the new roles without removing the old workflows

The first cutover saved a restricted pre-change configuration copy, checked its hash, and ran the external USB backup. The merged configuration passed OpenClaw’s schema validator before it replaced the live file.

We added 31 role entries, each with its own workspace and state directory. Their per-role settings included a Docker sandbox, no sandbox network, read-only root and workspace access, dropped capabilities, resource limits, and denied shell execution.

The existing main ID was wired to the eight department leads. Thirteen other legacy IDs, the Telegram binding, the documentation heartbeat, and the existing MCP server configuration were preserved. That made 45 registered IDs in total.

The gateway restart took about 35 seconds through plugin and channel startup. The direct health response and reliability monitor passed afterward. A live governance turn identified its role and refused the requested shell and host-file access. Inspecting its actual Docker container confirmed the recorded network, filesystem, capability, memory, and CPU restrictions.

The new per-role restrictions don’t establish that every legacy role or the preserved coordinator inherited the complete candidate policy. This was an additive cutover with targeted verification, not a clean replacement of all existing permissions.

Upgrade the runtime as a separate change

The next approved packet upgraded OpenClaw from 2026.10.4 to 2026.11.9. Beforehand, the daily OpenClaw backup and external USB copy had successful receipts.

Two admission blockers needed attention. An unused development symlink caused the candidate snapshot to be rejected; its target was recorded before removing the link. The expected policy-attestation hash also needed reconciliation with the verified post-cutover state. The recorded policy check passed all 68 checks before the upgrade proceeded.

Afterward, the installed version, live health, schema validation, reliability monitor, and a sandboxed governance turn were checked again. The 37-test adapter suite passed. The newer model entries appeared in the catalog.

One host result stayed separate: the daily AIDE file-integrity service reported failure after the approved changes. The upgrade receipt left that for an explicit baseline-review decision. It didn’t reinitialize the integrity database simply to clear the failure, and I can’t call that later checkpoint entirely clean.

Put the hybrid coordinator on the live route

I completed the official device-code authorization for the production coordinator. We didn’t copy the staging credentials into it.

main was configured for openai/gpt-6.2-sol through OpenClaw’s built-in runtime, with an empty fallback list. The default remained local ollama/qwen3:8b for the other 44 roles.

The smoke test recorded the expected cloud model and no fallback. The credential checks found no OAuth duplication in the 31 new role directories and no OpenAI API-key environment variable in the gateway process.

The decisive routing check used the live gateway: main delegated to local noc-lead in a restricted sandbox. A direct attempt to reach soc-tier1 was denied. Health and readiness passed, and the adapter suite passed again. The owner accepted these two final change packets on November 25.

Where this leaves the lab

The records show a production upgrade, an external backup with a selective restore, a functional database restore, new role boundaries, tested adapters, and a live hybrid delegation path. They don’t yet show every adapter used through a real Telegram request, a complete application recovery, or enabled production remediation.

The project scheduled a seven-day observation window from November 24 to December 1. As of this November 25 entry, that period hasn’t elapsed. The final acceptance needs the daily backup receipts and stability evidence, with material regressions investigated and the affected observation period reset where required.

The remaining list also includes the AIDE review, incomplete database dump coverage, no demonstrated WAL-based point-in-time recovery, the separately held recovery key, and the pending desktop-agent permission review. There is still one host and no failover.

That is the current stopping point for this series. The next post should come from what the lab actually does during the observation period: the scheduled jobs, any failures, the fixes, and the eventual acceptance decision.
entry.summary: The final changes added the new roles, upgraded OpenClaw, and proved a live cloud-to-local delegation. The observation period and recovery gaps remained open.

entry.title: Building security visibility that fit the laptop

link.title: Building security visibility that fit the laptop

entry.content:
Wazuh was part of the CyberBiota3.5 proposal. The machine’s resource budget decided whether it belonged in this implementation.

At the admission checkpoint, the Dell had about 12.2 GiB of available RAM. The project’s budget for the proposed Wazuh central stack was 8 GiB. Subtracting that left roughly 4.2 GiB—below the 8 GiB safety reserve and below the 6 GiB stop threshold.

We deferred it. The disk work had made room for files, but it hadn’t added RAM.

Use the security signals already present

CrowdSec and Alertmanager were running. The new security adapter queried their existing signals without enabling active response. Requests for Wazuh data returned a structured unavailable result because there was no Wazuh backend to query.

The vulnerability adapter read stored reports. It didn’t trigger an active scan. Case creation produced a draft, and the response interface produced a proposal awaiting approval, with executed: false.

Those distinctions mattered on a home lab carrying my apps and data. A security-related message was still data to inspect, not permission to change the firewall or stop a container.

The first security test set included malicious instructions embedded in tickets, cross-role access attempts, and input filtering for indicator lookups. Internal addresses, internal domains, and incident prose were rejected as external-enrichment inputs. The evidence here includes offline indicator fixtures; it doesn’t prove a complete live threat-intelligence service.

Test detection logic without claiming a sensor

We used benign positive and negative controls for detection handling. A matching sample had to appear, and a nonmatching control had to stay absent.

Later tests parsed offline EVE JSON and Zeek connection samples. The EVE test removed two raw-payload fields before returning a result. Connection summaries exposed metadata rather than packet contents.

Suricata wasn’t installed, and there was no switch-mirror feed. Passing these tests showed that the adapter handled those samples. It didn’t establish live network intrusion detection.

The live socket query had a different, narrower source: passive sockets on the Dell itself. Its result explicitly described local-host coverage. It couldn’t see all traffic crossing the home network, and we didn’t label it as if it could.

Inspect the endpoint without handing over a shell

The endpoint posture view gathered a fixed selection of information such as AppArmor status, failed units, and the state of existing security services. The investigation adapter used pre-approved packs for listening ports, container digests, privileged containers, and systemd timers.

The live container review still found two privileged containers and seven using host networking. The new agent sandboxes didn’t remove those existing exceptions. Keeping the exceptions in the record prevents a successful sandbox test from turning into a claim that the whole Docker estate has the same isolation.

Forensic handling was tested with a benign collection manifest and SHA-256 verification. The result returned evidence metadata rather than raw contents. That was a controlled test of the metadata path, not an investigation of an actual compromise.

What remained outside this upgrade

We also deferred Security Onion, Arkime, Graylog, Greenbone/OpenVAS, MISP, Fleet, Velociraptor, and Shuffle. Some would need substantially more resources; others would need a separate justification, target scope, or execution authorization.

The delivered work was smaller and more specific: existing security-signal queries, draft cases, bounded posture and investigation helpers, and tests that distinguished live data from offline samples. CyberBiota3.5 did not become a complete SIEM or an autonomous response platform during these three days.
entry.summary: The security work used existing signals and bounded investigations. The RAM calculation kept Wazuh out, and offline detection samples stayed clearly labeled.

entry.title: CyberBiota3.5 started with the lab I already had

link.title: CyberBiota3.5 started with the lab I already had

entry.content:
I started home labbing because I wanted to use open-source technology to host my own apps and keep my own data. AriseOne was the beginning. CyberBiota 1 and 2 gave me room to try different versions of the lab. CyberBiota3 brought those earlier lessons together.

CyberBiota3.5 builds on that same lab. The work recorded here happened over November 23–25, 2026: checking the host, repairing existing faults, testing a new agent structure, improving recovery, and putting the approved changes into production. I worked with coding agents on the implementation. The decisions, approvals, test results, and failures were recorded as we went.

The plan reached beyond the agent registry

The November 22 plan had two connected aims. OpenClaw would coordinate work on the home lab, while Addie 3 would bring together personal knowledge, planning, research, and selected actions. It covered the frontends, model routes, retrieval and memory, tools, identity, automation, monitoring, and recovery around that assistant.

The implementation records from the following days are more specific: host repairs, the operations roles, subscription-backed inference, read-only and draft adapters, recovery tests, and the live gateway changes. They don’t establish that the whole personal-assistant and second-brain plan was delivered. This series follows the work we can trace through those records; the broader plan remains context for where it is meant to lead.

Start by finding out what is actually running

The first inspection found 98 containers: 70 running, 25 exited, two created, and one restarting. That last one was Authelia, the authentication service. Its crash loop was also making the authenticated proxy check fail, even though OpenClaw’s own health endpoint still responded.

The machine was a Dell G7 7700 with a six-core, twelve-thread i7, about 30 GiB of usable RAM, and an RTX 2070 with 8 GiB of VRAM. It already ran the apps, databases, monitoring, and local inference. There wasn’t an empty server waiting for the new design.

The smaller system SSD was 87% full. The larger data SSD had about 1.2 TiB free. Fifty-three of the 70 running containers had no memory limit; 55 had no CPU limit. The repository backup service had failed on its last recorded run. Those findings determined the first changes.

The audit also corrected the paperwork. The monitoring backend was VictoriaMetrics, with vmalert, Alertmanager, Grafana, Loki, Alloy, and Blackbox Exporter. We didn’t need to install another monitoring stack just because an older plan named one. NetBox and CrowdSec were already running too.

Keep the upgrade inside this machine’s limits

I ruled out adding the second laptop to this build. Its inspection showed a two-core, four-thread processor, about 14 GiB of RAM, Wi-Fi connectivity, and no available KVM device. The approved project stayed on the Dell.

I also confirmed Qwen3 as the local model. An earlier proposal referred to a model that wasn’t installed. Ollama was actually serving qwen3:8b, and the first GPU snapshot showed it using about 6.6 GiB of the 8 GiB available. That made concurrent local inference a real capacity question.

The new design separated the work into 32 named roles across operations, security, databases, recovery, and the AI platform, with a coordinator and an independent governance role. These were identities with different permissions. They weren’t 32 models loaded into memory. Local reasoning started serially, and specialists were intended to run when needed.

Build beside production, then cross over deliberately

The early phases used separate state directories, an offline candidate configuration, and a loopback-only staging gateway. The existing OpenClaw gateway, Telegram binding, and legacy agents stayed in place while we tested.

By November 24, the new roles had been added to production. On November 25, OpenClaw had been upgraded and the live coordinator was using the approved OpenAI subscription route while the other roles stayed on local Qwen3. An allowed delegation succeeded; an attempt to skip the department lead was denied.

There is still a difference between reaching that point and finishing every part of the larger vision. The adapter suite was tested separately from the live gateway routing. Automatic production remediation remained disabled. Heavy security platforms were deferred, and the seven-day observation period was still underway when I wrote this.

The posts that follow trace the actual work: the clock and container repairs, the external backup, the failed local delegation test, the monitoring interfaces, the database restore, the incident drills, and the final cutover. That is the November upgrade I can show from the records.
entry.summary: The November upgrade began with an audit of a working home lab: one laptop, crowded storage, a local model, and several problems to fix before building on it.

entry.title: Getting a backup off the host—and restoring from it

link.title: Getting a backup off the host—and restoring from it

entry.content:
The first CyberBiota3.5 audit found several successful backup jobs. It also found that the verified copies were on the same Dell that ran the lab.

A local backup could help with a bad configuration or a damaged file. It didn’t give me a verified recovery copy outside the host. We kept that gap open while preparing the upgrade, then added an encrypted Restic repository on the external USB drive, under the name CyberBiota_Ark.

Preserve the drive’s existing files

The USB drive already contained my files. The approved work created a new backup repository in its own directory. It didn’t format the drive or remove what was there.

The backup covered the new 3.5 project records, selected Compose configuration, scripts, and the latest verified daily OpenClaw backup archive. Staging directories and selected sensitive or runtime files were excluded. That scope matters: this was not a complete image of the machine or a backup of every application’s data.

Restic encrypted the repository. The job obtained its credentials through the established secret-management arrangement without writing values into its receipts. The remaining recovery requirement was to keep a usable copy of the repository password outside the Dell. Losing the host must not also mean losing the only way to decrypt the external copy.

The disconnected-drive test came first

During the power and SSD work, the USB drive was disconnected. The backup script was tested in that state and returned its designated skip code without writing into the root filesystem.

That guard prevents a particular failure: a missing external mount can otherwise leave an ordinary directory at the expected path, allowing a job to fill the internal disk while appearing to write to USB. The service checked both the mountpoint and the expected backup directory before proceeding.

After the drive was reconnected, the first recorded run processed about 355 MiB across 13,015 files. It exited successfully, and restic check reported no errors. Starting the service separately also succeeded under its memory and CPU limits.

Bring files back from the external copy

We then restored two selected project files from the USB repository into a private staging directory on the data SSD. Their SHA-256 hashes matched the originals. The measured selective restore took 1.07 seconds, and the temporary directory was removed after verification.

That is a small but concrete test. The files came from the external repository, decrypted, and matched. The 1.07-second figure is the time for those selected files. It is not the recovery time for CyberBiota, its databases, or replacement hardware.

The separate database exercise later in this series went further: it started an isolated PostgreSQL instance and restored a database into it. Each test answered a different recovery question.

Check an unattended run as well

The USB job was scheduled for 04:15, with up to two minutes of randomized delay and a persistent systemd timer. The service was configured to skip when the drive was unavailable.

Enabling that timer wasn’t the last piece of evidence. The November 25 upgrade receipt recorded an automatic run at 04:17 and a clean repository check. That showed the scheduled path had actually run, beyond the earlier manual service test.

CyberBiota_Ark gave this upgrade an external encrypted recovery copy and a verified selective restore. It remains an attached USB backup rather than an offsite or continuously offline copy. Full host-loss recovery still needs replacement hardware, the separately held key, the missing application coverage, and a wider recovery exercise.
entry.summary: We added an encrypted repository to an existing USB drive, checked restored files, and verified the overnight backup job.
